accuracy.evidence: Matches the topic statement (recognise how deliberate choices of words, structure and tone create effects) and the KS2 reading aims to discuss words and phrases that capture the reader's interest and imagination. Verb meanings (crept, raced, limped, stomped, gobbled), connotation pairs (curious/nosy, slim/skinny, determined/stubborn) and the pace effect of short versus long sentences were checked against Oxford Learner's Dictionary definitions and standard writing guidance.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets three documented slips for 7 to 9 year olds: treating near-synonyms as interchangeable (nosy vs curious), assuming short sentences are always better (the bedtime round makes the long sentence the right answer), and answering 'why this word' by repeating the word instead of naming its effect (mastery m5). The adult text names all three as common mistakes.

lab_distinct.evidence: The mechanism is word swapping with an instant change in the scene: the dog's speed and gait follow the chosen verb, the sky darkens and a moon, owl and black cat appear as spooky words are picked, Sam's face changes with the connotation, and a heartbeat line shows the pace of the chosen version. Passed the 30% shingle gate against every other lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step isolates one authorial tool in the order a reader meets them: verb choice, mood words, connotation, sentence length, then explaining a choice. The learner sees the effect on the canvas first (the dog creeping, the night turning spooky) and the step message then names the rule.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions with tempting wrong options: 'Walked and raced both say the dog moved. Same picture?' (yes, moving is moving), 'Can three words turn a happy night spooky?' (no, you need a new story) and 'Do nosy and curious make you feel the same about Sam?' (yes, they mean the same). Each is disproved by the task and the reveal quotes the learner's guess.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating challenge questions; every wrong option carries a tag with its own message: plain word ('does not paint a strong picture'), opposite feeling, 'authors choose each word on purpose' for the random-choice belief, the unkind-synonym message for Ben, and the pace message for the long scary sentence. Lab steps give per-option feedback too (SLOTWHY, KINDWHY, WHY).

readability.evidence: Kid explanation is short sentences of common words with the examples shown, not described; it passes the family FK gate well under 5. Canvas text uses at most one short sentence per card and the example lines (The wind howled round the house) are decodable for ages 7 to 9.

no_filler.evidence: Content gate found no filler phrases and duplication against other lessons stays under 12%. Every kid paragraph carries a worked example (walked/raced/crept, curious/nosy, Run. Now. Go!) and the adult text is limited to tools, lab actions, mistakes and one home prompt.

mobile.evidence: Walked on iPhone 13 and desktop: six steps, five tasks and the challenge complete, each Show me reaching the tick inside 6 seconds. Screenshots at 390 px in dark theme showed word buttons at least 56 px tall in the young layout, the spooky scene and pace cards unclipped, and the dog staying inside the canvas.

accessibility.evidence: axe reported no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in light or dark theme. Every canvas target has a matching HTML button (words, rows, Version A/B, answer letters with full-text aria-labels), and the canvas aria-label is updated with the current sentence, chosen words and progress after every action.
